# STM32H743 Nano FC + 4-in-1 ESC: Power-Stage Thermal Model and Bidirectional DShot600 Timer/DMA Architecture

## 0. Assumptions and Architecture Notes

There is no published "Job #45" spec, so every number below rests on the stated assumptions. Replace them with your actual BOM values and rerun the equations.

**Architecture.** In a 4-in-1 ESC, the 48 kHz commutation PWM is generated by each ESC's own MCU, not the H743. That MCU is typically an STM32G071 or AT32F421 running AM32 or BLHeli_32. The H743 only sends the DShot600 command stream and decodes the bidirectional eRPM telemetry. The model is split along that boundary.

**Baseline parameters**

| Parameter | Symbol | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Bus voltage (6S, full charge) | V_bus | 25.2 V |
| Burst phase current per ESC | I_pk | 80 A |
| ESC PWM frequency | f_sw | 48 kHz |
| MOSFET R_DS(on) @ 25 °C, V_GS=10 V | R_25 | 1.0 mΩ (40 V, PDFN 3.3×3.3 or 5×6) |
| R_DS(on) temperature coefficient | k_T | ≈1.5× at T_j = 125 °C |
| Rise / fall time (with gate driver) | t_r, t_f | 20 ns / 20 ns |
| Dead time | t_dt | 200 ns per edge |
| Body-diode forward voltage | V_F | 0.8 V |
| Total gate charge | Q_g | 50 nC |
| Effective output charge | Q_oss | 40 nC |
| Gate drive voltage | V_GS | 10 V |
| Commutation scheme | — | 6-step trapezoidal with synchronous rectification (complementary PWM) |

---

## 1. Conduction Loss Model (80 A Burst)

### 1.1 Current path
In 6-step drive, at any instant one high-side leg is PWM-switching and one low-side leg is conducting. With complementary PWM, the PWM'd leg's high-side FET (duty D) and low-side FET (duty 1−D) share that phase current. As a result, two FET channel resistances are always in the motor current path, independent of duty:

$$P_{cond,ESC} = I_{rms}^2 \cdot 2R_{DS(on)}(T_j)$$

Phase current ripple at 48 kHz is small relative to 80 A for typical motor inductance (tens of µH), so I_rms ≈ I_pk.

### 1.2 Temperature-dependent R_DS(on)

$$R_{DS(on)}(T_j) = R_{25}\left[1 + \alpha (T_j - 25)\right],\quad \alpha \approx 0.005\ /°C$$

At T_j = 125 °C, R ≈ 1.5 mΩ.

$$P_{cond} = 80^2 \times 2 \times 1.5\,\text{m}\Omega = \mathbf{19.2\ W\ per\ ESC\ channel}$$

At a cold start (25 °C) the figure is 12.8 W. This is a positive-feedback loop, which section 4.3 addresses.

### 1.3 Per-FET distribution (worst case D ≈ 0.5)

| FET | Loss |
|---|---|
| PWM leg high side | I²R·D = 4.8 W |
| PWM leg low side (sync rect) | I²R·(1−D) = 4.8 W |
| Static low side (other phase) | I²R per 1/3 of electrical cycle ≈ 9.6 W during its conduction interval |

The commutating low-side FET is the hot spot. Averaged over rotation, each of the 6 FETs dissipates about 19.2/6 × (duty share) ≈ 3.2 W. The static-low FET sees 9.6 W pulses at the electrical frequency. At typical eRPM (≥ 1 kHz electrical), these pulses are well below the junction thermal time constant (~ms), so the average applies.

### 1.4 PCB copper loss (often ignored, but not negligible)
Assume a 2 oz outer layer plus 2 oz inner layers in parallel. The effective phase-path resistance is about 0.3–0.5 mΩ.

$$P_{Cu} = 80^2 \times 0.4\,\text{m}\Omega \approx 2.6\ \text{W per channel}$$

---

## 2. Switching Loss Model at 48 kHz

Only one leg switches per ESC at a time.

### 2.1 Hard-switching V–I overlap

$$P_{VI} = \tfrac{1}{2} V_{bus} I (t_r + t_f) f_{sw} = 0.5 \times 25.2 \times 80 \times 40\text{ns} \times 48\text{k} = \mathbf{1.94\ W}$$

### 2.2 Dead-time body-diode conduction

$$P_{dt} = V_F \cdot I \cdot 2t_{dt} \cdot f_{sw} = 0.8 \times 80 \times 400\text{ns} \times 48\text{k} = \mathbf{1.23\ W}$$

### 2.3 Reverse recovery
Body-diode Q_rr for 40 V trench FETs is about 30–60 nC at high di/dt.

$$P_{rr} \approx Q_{rr} V_{bus} f_{sw} = 50\text{nC} \times 25.2 \times 48\text{k} = 0.06\ \text{W}$$

### 2.4 Output capacitance

$$P_{oss} = \tfrac{1}{2} Q_{oss} V_{bus} f_{sw} \approx 0.5 \times 40\text{nC} \times 25.2 \times 48\text{k} = 0.024\ \text{W}$$

### 2.5 Gate drive
This loss lands in the driver and gate resistors, not the FETs.

$$P_{gate} = Q_g V_{GS} f_{sw} \times 2\ \text{(switching pair)} = 50\text{nC}\times10\times48\text{k}\times2 = 0.048\ \text{W}$$

### 2.6 Frequency sensitivity
The 48 kHz choice is about 3.3 W of the per-channel budget. At 24 kHz this halves to about 1.6 W, at the cost of audible whine and more current ripple. Total switching loss scales with frequency as:

$$P_{sw}(f) \approx 6.9\times10^{-5}\cdot f \quad [\text{W}, f\ \text{in Hz}]$$

---

## 3. Total Burst Power Budget

| Loss term | Per ESC | ×4 |
|---|---|---|
| Conduction (T_j = 125 °C) | 19.2 W | 76.8 W |
| PCB copper | 2.6 W | 10.4 W |
| V–I switching | 1.94 W | 7.8 W |
| Dead-time diode | 1.23 W | 4.9 W |
| Q_rr + Q_oss + gate | 0.13 W | 0.5 W |
| Bus capacitor ESR (see 3.1) | 0.8 W | 3.2 W |
| **Total** | **≈ 25.9 W** | **≈ 104 W** |

**Efficiency check.** Output power is roughly 25.2 V × 80 A × D. At D = 1 that is 2016 W per channel, giving about 98.7 % efficiency. At D = 0.5 it drops to about 97.4 %.

### 3.1 Bus capacitor ripple

$$I_{C,rms} = I\sqrt{D(1-D)} \le 0.5 I = 40\ \text{A}_{rms}\ \text{per ESC}$$

With phase-staggered PWM across the 4 ESCs (if the firmware supports it), the combined ripple drops toward 40 A × √4 / 4 ≈ 20 A rms. Otherwise, the worst case adds coherently. With a local MLCC bank of about 0.5 mΩ ESR per channel, P ≈ 0.8 W.
